shots: a sunny backyard family cookout, a 24 year old African American young woman with warm brown skin, a bright smile and shoulder length natural curly hair, wearing a yellow sweatshirt laughing and telling a story while relatives around a picnic table laugh with her, string lights, grill smoke

shots.en: Everybody called my cousin Sunshine. If you were down, she'd find you.
She showed up for everybody.

shots: a 24 year old African American young woman with warm brown skin, a bright smile and shoulder length natural curly hair, wearing a yellow sweatshirt fixing the collar of a nervous friend in a dress shirt outside an office building, both smiling, morning light

shots.en: You got this. Walk in there like you already work there.
She was the one hyping you up before the interview. Every time.

shots: a 24 year old African American young woman with warm brown skin, a bright smile and shoulder length natural curly hair, wearing a yellow sweatshirt sitting on a city bus looking at her phone with a quick forced smile, the screen not visible, afternoon light through the window

shots.en: I texted her that week. You good? She sent back, lol, I'm good. With the laughing face.
I believed her. We all did.

shots: a dark bedroom at night lit only by blue window light, a 24 year old African American young woman with warm brown skin and shoulder length natural curly hair, wearing a gray oversized t-shirt sitting alone on the floor with her back against the bed and her knees pulled up, a phone face down on the carpet beside her, heavy quiet mood, nothing else on the floor

shots.en: What we didn't see was how heavy it had gotten.
Bright people learn to hide dark rooms.

shots: a bedroom doorway at night, a 10 year old African American boy in blue pajamas standing in the doorway holding a pillow, sleepy and scared, soft hallway light behind him

shots.en: Sunny? I had a bad dream. Can I sleep in here?
Yeah. Come on.

shots: dim bedroom at night, a 10 year old African American boy in blue pajamas lying in bed under a blanket talking with his hands, a 24 year old African American young woman with warm brown skin and shoulder length natural curly hair, wearing a gray oversized t-shirt lying beside him listening, soft blue light

shots.en: It was a big dog, but it was a nice dog. Can we get a dog? A real one?
And Mr. Grant said my volcano was the best one in the class.
You're my favorite person. Don't tell Mom.

shots: close up of a 24 year old African American young woman with warm brown skin and shoulder length natural curly hair, wearing a gray oversized t-shirt lying awake on a pillow at night staring at the ceiling, a single tear on her cheek, a sleeping 10 year old boy's head resting on her arm, blue light

shots.en: She didn't sleep. She just lay there, with him on her arm.
He didn't know it, but he was holding the door open.

shots: gray early dawn light in a bedroom, a 24 year old African American young woman with warm brown skin and shoulder length natural curly hair, wearing a gray oversized t-shirt sitting up in bed holding a phone with both hands, typing, a 10 year old boy still asleep beside her, the screen not visible

shots.en: Mama, can you come in here. I'm not okay. I need help.
She hit send. That was the bravest thing I ever saw anybody do.

shots: dawn light in a bedroom, a 52 year old African American mother with short gray-streaked natural hair, wearing a robe kneeling beside the bed with her arms wrapped tightly around a 24 year old African American young woman with warm brown skin and shoulder length natural curly hair, wearing a gray oversized t-shirt, both eyes closed, a 10 year old boy asleep in the background

shots.en: Footsteps in the hall. Right away.
I'm here, baby. I'm right here. We're gonna get you help. You're not by yourself.

shots: a calm bright afternoon, a 24 year old African American young woman with warm brown skin, a bright smile and shoulder length natural curly hair, wearing a yellow sweatshirt sitting on a wooden bench outside a small brick counseling office building with a Bible open on her lap and a notebook beside her, gentle hopeful expression, no readable text

shots.en: Elijah sat under a tree and told God he was done. God didn't argue with him.
He sent an angel to wake him up and said, Arise and eat; the journey is too great for thee.
He didn't say be stronger. He said eat, sleep, let somebody help you. And then, one more day.

shots: close up of an open notebook on a wooden bench in sunlight beside an open Bible, a woman's hand holding a pen, handwritten list lines not readable, warm hopeful light

shots.en: Theo's dog. Sunday dinner. Finish my degree. One more day.
The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart. Psalm thirty four, eighteen.
In real life, our Sunshine didn't get her knock.
So we built a door that's always open.
For our Sunshine.
If you're carrying something heavy tonight, tell one person. A text is enough.
In the United States, call or text nine eight eight, any time.
Anywhere else, find a free line in your country at find a helpline dot com. If you're in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

shots: a young African American woman with natural curly hair sitting by a sunny window holding a phone, a calm small smile, a cup of tea on the sill, no readable text

shots.en: Community Covenant has an Ask for Help button. You don't have to explain everything. A real person from our team reads every message and writes back.
There are Wisdom Reels with Scripture read aloud for heavy nights, and prayer from people who mean it.
You are not alone. Keep pushing one more day. Don't give up in God.
Get Community Covenant at covenant dot crispusmundo dot com.

shots: a dark kitchen at 2 in the morning, a 40 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a neat low bun in a bathrobe sitting at the table lit by her phone screen, reading with a stunned face, the screen not visible

shots.en: Hey sis. Not trying to dig up the past. I've moved on, and I hope you have too. God bless!
Six years. And that's what you send me.

shots: a hospital surgery waiting room, a 40 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a neat low bun sitting alone in a chair with a newborn baby asleep in an infant car seat carrier at her feet, tired worried face, fluorescent light, clock on the wall

shots.en: Mama's surgery. My baby was nine days old.
I sat in that room for eleven hours. My sister lived twenty minutes away.
I texted her. Are you coming? Delivered. Read. Nothing.

shots: night in a hospital waiting room, a 40 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a neat low bun looking at her phone with tears in her eyes, the baby carrier beside her, empty chairs, the screen not visible

shots.en: That night, she posted pictures from a party.

shots: a dark kitchen at 2 in the morning, a 40 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a neat low bun typing angrily on her phone with both thumbs, jaw set, a cold cup of tea, the screen not visible

shots.en: You moved on? I never got the chance. I'm not doing this again.
I typed it. I didn't send it.

shots: a 40 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a neat low bun at a kitchen table at night reading an open Bible under a small lamp, her phone set aside, thoughtful tired face

shots.en: Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way. First be reconciled to thy brother.
Lord, I've been trying to be reconciled for six years. You can't reconcile with God bless.

shots: a 40 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a neat low bun calm now at the kitchen table at dawn, typing carefully on her phone, a Bible open beside her, soft gray light, the screen not visible

shots.en: I don't need you to prove yourself. I need you to be honest. You weren't there when I needed my sister most.
Until you can say that out loud, God bless isn't reconciliation. It's a door you're holding shut while you ask me to walk through it.
I love you. I'm not closing the door. But I won't pretend it didn't happen.

shots: a 40 year old African American woman nurse with brown skin and her hair in a neat low bun, wearing navy blue scrubs on break in a hospital break room, looking down at a phone ringing in her hand, surprised and nervous, vending machine behind her

shots.en: Three days later. Not a text. A call.

shots: a 37 year old African American woman with long sleek straight hair, polished makeup and a camel blazer sitting in a parked car holding a phone to her ear, eyes wet, no makeup smile, humble, a real estate sign on the back seat, overcast light

shots.en: You're right. I wasn't there.
I was scared of that hospital. And I was jealous of how everybody leaned on you, so I hid behind being busy.
That was wrong. I'm sorry.

shots: close up of a 40 year old African American woman nurse with brown skin and her hair in a neat low bun, wearing navy blue scrubs holding a phone to her ear with her eyes closed, letting out a long breath, a small relieved trembling smile, hospital break room

shots.en: Thank you for saying it.
Can we start small?
Coffee. Sunday. You're buying.

shots: a cozy coffee shop on a Sunday, two African American sisters sitting at a small table, a 40 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a neat low bun in a sweater and a 37 year old African American woman with long sleek straight hair, polished makeup and a camel blazer, a little awkward, the younger sister sliding a coffee cup across the table, the older one almost smiling

shots.en: Trust isn't handed back in one phone call. It's rebuilt, one honest cup of coffee at a time.
But it can't start until somebody tells the truth.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins. First John one, nine.

shots: a 40 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a neat low bun on a couch in the evening with a phone in her hand, calm, a warm lamp beside her, the screen not visible

shots.en: Somebody owe you an apology they may never give? Or do you owe one you don't know how to start?
In Community Covenant, the Wisdom Reels on forgiveness walk you through it with Scripture read aloud.
Tap Ask for Help, and a real person from our team writes back and prays with you.
Forgiveness is free. Trust is rebuilt. Get Community Covenant at covenant dot crispusmundo dot com.
